## feature

### Calibration-aware approval, stricter validation, new metrics

```
level: high
```

#### reason

Every behavior change has a dedicated regression test, including the reviewer's counterexamples, and the full suite plus type checks pass after the changes.

#### description

```
type: [text]
```

1. Comparisons carry `threshold_calibrated`; a PASS against an uncalibrated threshold withholds approval (REVIEW + `TECH_THRESHOLD_UNCALIBRATED` finding), per spec §7 "configured or calibrated".
2. Strict policy validation: real booleans, finite non-negative maxima, known `(metric, method)` pairs, string-list selectors, overlapping-scope duplicate rules rejected (disjoint per-profile repeats allowed).
3. CASAVA mate-number parsing with cross-file and within-header contradiction checks.
4. BAM `SM` reconciliation with the manifest, undefined-RG record counter, clipping summaries (full scan), and joint read-length × mean-quality summaries (sample-based, FASTQ and BAM).
5. `merge_rate` preferred over `merge_retained_fraction`; optional fastp evidence is `NOT_ASSESSED` unless required.
6. BAM metric selection by profile — insert-size only for `paired_short`; `n_content` added for BAM.

#### before

Uncalibrated thresholds approved pooling; a quoted `calibrated: "false"` silently became true; swapped CASAVA annotations, header/manifest sample conflicts, and unpaired-BAM insert demands all passed unnoticed.

#### after

Approval requires calibrated thresholds; malformed or contradictory policy and input metadata fail loudly; inapplicable evidence never blocks; two spec §6 metrics that were missing are now present.

#### evidence

```
level: high
type: [text]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

- `tests/test_policy.py::test_uncalibrated_threshold_prevents_automatic_approval`, `test_policy_load_and_strictness` (boolean/finiteness/method/overlap rejections).
- `tests/test_fastq.py::test_swapped_casava_mate_annotations_rejected`, `test_uniform_high_quality_phred33_accepted`.
- `tests/test_policy.py::test_bam_conflicting_sm_values_are_identity_conflict`, `test_bam_sm_mismatching_manifest_is_review`, `test_bam_undefined_rg_records_reported`.
- `tests/test_e2e.py::test_ont_bam_group_has_no_insert_size_requirement` (also asserts joint and clipping rows exist).

:::

## fix

### BAM reservoir was quadratic; 165× slower than necessary

```
level: high
```

#### reason

A direct re-profile on the same 500k-record file before and after the fix shows 368 → 61,246 records/s, and a regression test proves batched and single-row updates produce identical samples.

#### description

```
type: [statistic]
```

1. `FeatureReservoir.add_block` sorted the whole retained array on every update; the BAM path called it once per accepted record, so filling a reservoir of size k cost O(k² log k).
2. The reservoir now defers sorting to `sample()` (partition selection keeps the k-smallest set; the k-th smallest comes from a partition max), and the BAM scanner batches accepted candidates in chunks of 4096.
3. Measured on the benchmark file: 500,000 records in 8.164 s (61,246 rec/s), previously 1,360.5 s (368 rec/s).

#### before

A 500k-record BAM scan took 22 minutes, and the README wrongly attributed the cost to pysam.

#### after

The same scan takes 8 seconds, and the bottleneck documentation states what measurement now supports: pysam per-record access dominates, at roughly half the FASTQ rate.

#### evidence

```
level: high
type: [statistic]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

- `benchmarks/results-2026-10-21.json`: `bam` entry wall 8.164 s (re-run 2026-10-21T17:02+0800, same host and file as the 1,360.5 s entry in the prior measurement).
- `tests/test_sampling.py::test_batched_and_single_updates_give_identical_samples`.

:::

### Output collision protection missed consumed inputs

```
level: high
```

#### reason

Three new path tests demonstrate the rejection for manifest, policy, and fastp-report collisions, including with `--overwrite` supplied.

#### description

```
type: [text]
```

1. `validate_output_paths` received only `path1`/`path2`; the manifest, policy, and fastp reports were unprotected, so `--metrics-out <manifest> --overwrite` would destroy the manifest at publish time.
2. The pipeline now passes every consumed input into the collision check.

#### before

An output path equal to the manifest or policy was accepted and could overwrite the input after a successful run.

#### after

The run aborts with `output path ... collides with an input file` before any scanning.

#### evidence

```
level: high
type: [text]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

`tests/test_outputs_errors.py::test_output_colliding_with_manifest_rejected_even_with_overwrite`, `..._with_policy_rejected`, `..._with_fastp_report_rejected`.

:::

## limitation

### Uncalibrated shipped policy can never approve

```
level: high
```

#### reason

This is now enforced behavior with tests and updated examples, so the boundary is certain; it is listed because users must understand it before relying on outcomes.

#### description

```
type: [text]
```

1. The shipped example policy marks every threshold `calibrated: false`, so its groups can never reach COMPATIBLE — they end in REVIEW with `TECH_THRESHOLD_UNCALIBRATED` findings.
2. This follows the specification's rule that uncalibrated thresholds must not automatically approve pooling.
3. All eight examples were regenerated and now show these corrected outcomes.

#### evidence

```
level: high
type: [text]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

`examples/run_examples.sh` output 2026-10-21: scenarios 1–5 and 8 → REVIEW; 6 → INCOMPATIBLE; 7 → INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE. README "Examples" section updated.

:::

## caveat

### Phred+64 detection remains a heuristic

```
level: medium
```

#### reason

The tightened bound (min ≥ 64 AND max ≥ 90) accepts the reviewer's uniform-Q42 counterexample and still rejects classic Phred+64 files, but ASCII-range overlap zones are inherently undecidable; the README documents both bounds.

#### description

```
type: [text]
```

1. Bytes outside [33, 126] always abort.
2. The ambiguity heuristic now requires the classic signature: no byte below `@` (64) and some byte at or above `Z` (90) — Q57+ is impossible under Phred+33 on real platforms, while Q26 under Phred+64 is routine.
3. A file confined to bytes 64–89 remains ambiguous and is accepted as Phred+33, per the specification's instruction not to pretend ranges can always distinguish encodings.

#### evidence

```
level: high
type: [text]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

`tests/test_fastq.py::test_uniform_high_quality_phred33_accepted` (all-`K` accepted), `test_likely_phred64_rejected` (bytes up to 104 still rejected), `src/seqconsistency/fastq.py` module docstring and `LIKELY_P64_*` constants.

:::

## assumption

### Reviewer disagreements resolved without new work

```
level: medium
```

#### reason

The two disagreements rest on the specification text itself, which is in the record; no evidence contradicts them.

#### description

```
type: [text]
```

1. Sourmash and coverage comparison remain unimplemented: the specification marks both Phase-2 optional, and the README/decisions state they are absent.
2. `merge_retained_fraction` keeps its name and semantics (after/before); `merge_rate` was added as the preferred comparison when explicit merged-read counts exist, rather than replacing a correctly labeled metric.

## conclusion

### The review round improved correctness and removed the dominant performance defect

```
level: high
```

#### reason

All agreed items are implemented with regression tests, the suite is green, and the re-measured benchmark quantifies the improvement on identical inputs.

#### description

```
type: [text]
```

1. Approval semantics now match the specification for uncalibrated thresholds; three false-approval and false-rejection paths are closed.
2. Input destruction via output collision is impossible for every consumed input.
3. BAM scanning is 166× faster on the measured workload, and the committed bottleneck claim now matches measurement.

#### evidence

```
level: high
type: [statistic]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

Final suite exit 0 (`/tmp/final_suite2.log`); `benchmarks/results-2026-10-21.{json,md}` re-measured 17:02+0800; mypy and ruff clean.

:::

level: high
```

#### reason

#### description

```

```

| Workload | Before fix | After fix |
|---|---:|---:|
| SE FASTQ 2M×100 bp | 119,977 reads/s | 124,660 reads/s |

### discarded a contaminated benchmark run, then re-ran clean

```
status: right
```

#### description

```
type: [text]
```

1. The first post-fix benchmark started while tests were still running, which would have contended the CPU.
2. It was killed and re-run after the machine went idle; the committed numbers come from the clean run.

```

### initially attributed the BAM slowness to pysam without profiling

```
status: wrong
```

#### description

```
type: [text]
```

1. The MVP report stated pysam object creation dominated BAM scanning — asserted from plausibility, not measurement.
2. The reviewer's micro-benchmark challenged it; profiling after the reservoir fix showed the quadratic reservoir update was the real cost (368 → 61k rec/s with pysam unchanged).
3. The better action, now applied: profile before writing any bottleneck claim, and record the correction in the benchmark document.

#### evidence

```
level: high
type: [statistic]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

`benchmarks/results-2026-10-21.md` bottleneck note 3; direct re-profile on `/tmp/seqc-bench/bench.bam` (8.2 s for 500k records).

:::
